passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.title: The Kybalion

From the Absolute point of view, there is nothing Real except THE ALL, no matter what terms we may use in thinking of, o
passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.title: The Kybalion

Oh, friends, to mortals this Universe of Mentality is very real indeed--it is

What is IN THE INFINITE MIND OF THE ALL is REAL in a degree second only to that Rea
passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.context: How often have the majority of people heard repeated the statement that their Deity (called by many names) was "All in All" and how little have they suspected the inner occult truth concealed by these carelessly uttered words? And, this being so, let us seek this truth, the understanding of which mea
passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.context: We have given you the Hermetic Teaching regarding the Mental Nature of the Universe--the truth that "the Universe is Mental--held in the Mind of THE ALL." As the Kybalion says, in the passage quoted above: "All is in THE ALL." But note also the co-related statement, that: "It is equally true that THE ALL is in ALL." passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.context: The Hermetic Teachings are to the effect that THE ALL is Imminent in ("remaining within; inherent; abiding within") its Universe, and in every part, particle, unit, or combination, within the Universe. This statement is usually illustrated by the Teachers by a reference to the Principle of Correspondence. The Teacher instructs the student to form a Mental Image of something, a person, an idea, something having a mental form, the favorite example being that of the author or dr
passages.title: The Kybalion

Whose is the "spirit" of the characters that we know as Micawber, Oliver Twist, Uriah Heep--is it Dickens, or have each of these characters a personal spirit, independent of their creator? Have
passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.context: And, in the degree that Man realizes the existence of the Indwelling Spirit immanent within his being, so will he rise in the spiritual scale of life. This is what spiritual development means--the recognition, realization, and manifestation of the Spirit within us. Try to remember this last definition--that of spiritual development. It contains the Truth of True Religion.
passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.context: There are many planes of Being--many sub-planes of Life--many degrees of existence in the Universe. passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.context: The Hermetic Teachings concerning the process of the Mental Creation of the Universe, are that at the beginning of the Creative Cycle, THE ALL, in its aspect of Being, projects its Will toward its aspect of "Becoming" and the process of creation begins. This process is called the stage of
passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.context: This Involuntary stage of Creation is sometimes called the "Outpouring" of the Divine Energy, just as the Evolutionary state is called the "Indrawing." The extreme pole of the Creative process is considered to be the furthest removed from THE ALL, while the beginning of the Evolutionary stage is regarded as the beginning of the return swing of the pendulum of Rhythm--a "coming home" idea being held in all of the Hermetic Teachings.
passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.context: The Teachings are that during the "Outpouring," the vibrations become lower and lower until finally the urge ceases, and the return swing begins. But there is this difference, that while in the "Outpouring" the creative forces manifest compactly and as a whole, yet from the beginning of the Evolutionary or "Indrawing" stage, there is manifested the Law of Individualization--that is, the tendency to separate into Units of Force, so that finally that which left THE ALL as unind
passages.title: The Kybalion

But the idea intended seems to be that of the employment of the Divine Attention. passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.context: There is one more matter of which we desire to speak in this lesson, and that comes very near to an invasion of the Metaphysical field of speculation, although our purpose is merely to show the futility of such speculation. The question is: "WHY does THE ALL create Universes" The question may be asked in different forms, but the above is the gist of the inquiry.

passages.context: Men have striven hard to answer this question, but still there is no answer worthy of the name. Some have imagined that THE ALL had something to gain by it, but this is absurd, for what could THE ALL gain that it did not already possess? passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.title: The Kybalion

So, you see, the matter is Unthinkable, just as THE ALL is Unknowable. Just as we say THE ALL merely "IS"--so we are compelled to say that "THE ALL ACTS BECAUSE IT ACTS." passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.context: The great Second Hermetic Principle embodies the truth that there is a harmony, agreement, and correspondence between the several planes of Manifestation, Life and Being. This truth is a truth because all that is included in the Universe emanates from the same source, and the same laws, principles, and characteristics apply to each unit, or combination of units, of activity, as each manifests its own phenomena upon its own plane.
passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.context: For the purpose of convenience of thought and study, the Hermetic Philosophy considers that the Universe may be divided into three great classes of phenomena, known as the Three Great Planes, namely:

passages.context: 1. The Great Physical Plane. 2. The Great Mental Plane. 3. The Great Spiritual Plane.
passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.context: These divisions are more or less artificial and arbitrary, for the truth is that all of the three divisions are but ascending degrees of the great scale of Life, the lowest point of which is undifferentiated Matter, and the highest point that of Spirit. passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.context: In short, the Three Great Planes may be regarded as three great groups of degrees of Life Manifestation. While the purposes of this little book do not allow us to enter into an extended discussion of, or explanation of, the subject of these different planes, still we think it well to give a general description of the same at this point.
passages.title: The Kybalion

The degree
passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.context: You will kindly remember, however, that the Three Great Planes are not actual divisions of the phenomena of the Universe, but merely arbitrary terms used by the Hermetists in order to aid in the thought and study of the various degrees and Forms of universal activity and life. passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.context: The Great Physical Plane, and its Seven Minor Planes, is that division of the phenomena of the Universe which includes all that relates to physics, or material things, forces, and manifestations. It includes all forms of that which we call Matter, and all forms of that which we call Energy or Force. passages.context: The Plane of Matter (A) comprises the forms of Matter in its form of solids, liquids, and gases, as generally recognized by the text-books on physics. passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.context: The Plane of Elemental Mind (C), in its seven sub-divisions, comprises those entities or beings, invisible as are all such elemental forms, which partake of the nature of both animal and human life in a degree and in certain combinations. The highest forms are semi-human in intelligence.
passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.context: The Plane of Human Mind, in its seven sub-divisions, comprises those manifestations of life and mentality which are common to Man, in his various grades, degrees, and divisions. passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.context: Passing on from the Great Mental Plane to the Great Spiritual Plane, what shall we say? How can we explain these higher states of Being, Life and Mind, to minds as yet unable to grasp and understand the higher subdivisions of the Plane of Human Mind? The task is impossible. We can speak only in the most general terms. How may Light be described to a man born blind--how sugar, to a man who has never tasted anything sweet--how harmony, to one born deaf?
passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.context: All that we can say is that the Seven Minor Planes of the Great Spiritual Plane (each Minor Plane having its seven sub-divisions) comprise Beings possessing Life, Mind and Form as far above that of Man of to-day as the latter is above the earth-worm, mineral or even certain forms of Energy or Matter. passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.context: Do not eat a plant you have not identified. Edible species can have toxic lookalikes. This is an offline caution, not a field guide or medical advice.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: Plantago, often called plantain, is a common lawn weed with parallel veins. Crushed plantain (Plantago) leaves are a traditional poultice for an itchy insect bite, and only after the plant is identified. Not a treatment.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: Willow bark (Salix) is traditionally used for aches, not as a medicine. Salicin from willow is described as an analgesic, and astringent tannins show up in the bark. Identify the tree before any use. This is not a dose or a substitute for emergency care.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: Milky sap, bulb leaves, or umbrella flower clusters are reasons to stop and not taste a plant. Cultivated food is safer than foraging when identification is uncertain.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: Yarrow (Achillea millefolium) is a field plant for a small bleeding scrape, and only after the plant is identified. Feathery leaves and a flat white flower cluster are the usual look, and lookalikes are easy to mistake. Do not use a plant you have not identified. This is not a dose or a substitute for emergency care.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: Biomes are broad living landscapes: forest, grassland, desert, tundra, and coast, set by climate and water more than by towns. Plants and the ground underfoot tell you which pattern you are in. A biome is not a line you can pace to a city limit. Weather still changes inside it.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: Terrain is the shape you walk: flat, rolling, steep, broken, swampy, or cliffed. Steep ground costs time. Broken rock hides ankles. Soft ground hides depth. Choose the line that keeps you on ground you can see. This is a travel cue, not a soil survey or a road map.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: A watershed is the land that drains to one stream, lake, or coast. Ridges are the divides. Water runs away from them into the basin. Following a creek downhill moves you toward that basin's trunk stream, not necessarily toward help. A drainage is not a trail.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: A coast is where land meets a large body of water. Tides, cliffs, and headlands change the walkable strip through the day. A headland is a natural landmark. A harbor town is not stored here. Stay off wet rock when the sea is rising, and do not guess a tide table you do not have.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: Mountains stack climate. Higher is usually colder, windier, and slower. A pass is a low saddle between higher ground. A peak is a landmark only while you can still see it. Weather arrives fast on ridges. Turn back when the route you can see runs out. This is not a climb grade.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: Deserts are water-poor landscapes, hot or cold, where shade and the water you carry matter more than speed. Washes can flood from rain you do not see. Walk the firm edge of a wash, not its throat. Do not chase a shimmer toward a town. Night can turn sharply cold.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: Forests hide the sun and the distant ridge. Travel is slower, and a handrail such as a stream or a ridge matters more than a bearing you cannot check. Moss is not a compass. Mark the way back while the last sure point is still in sight. This is not a timber or trail catalog.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: Arctic and tundra country is open, cold, and often wet underfoot, with few trees to use as landmarks. When the horizon disappears, a short bearing and a counted pace are safer than a long walk. Summer light can last all day. Winter dark does the opposite. Ice is not a path this note approves.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: River cues: a V of ripples often points at a rock, and smooth dark water can be deep. The outside of a bend cuts the bank. The inside piles gravel. Current is a force, not a trail. Wade only at a wide shallow place you have walked, and do not enter flood water.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: Useful landmarks are natural and stable: a peak, a saddle, a lone butte, a confluence, a waterfall, a headland, a lake outlet. Name them on the map you carry and in a waypoint you save yourself. This store has no city, street, or business directory. If the landmark clouds over, rejoin a handrail.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: Climate bands follow latitude and altitude in a rough way: tropical, subtropical, temperate, polar, plus dry belts where rain rarely falls. A band says what the season tends to do, not what tomorrow's storm will do. Height can copy a colder band. Watch the sky you actually have.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: Magnetic declination is the angle between magnetic north and true north at a place. It changes slowly over years and with where you stand. A compass needle points magnetic. A map's meridians are the true frame. Set the declination printed on your map before you trust a bearing. There is no live declination feed.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: True north follows the planet's axis, toward the geographic pole. Magnetic north is where the needle points, and the gap between them is declination. East declination means magnetic north sits east of true north. Add east declination to a magnetic bearing to plot true. A position lock is a point, not a north reference.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: Contour lines join points of equal elevation. Lines close together mean steep ground. Wide gaps mean flatter ground. A V in the contours often points upstream in a valley. Index contours are the labeled ones. They show shape, not a trail name. The interval is printed on the map you carry.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: Map and compass: set the map to the land, lay the compass edge on the line you mean to walk, turn the housing to north on the map, then turn your body until the needle agrees. Walk a short leg to a landmark you named and count paces. This is a method sketch, not a course certificate.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: Elevation is height above a datum, often mean sea level. A GPS altitude, when a consented fix includes one, is a rough height and is weaker than the horizontal fix. If the lock has no altitude, say so and do not invent one. Contours show shape. A barometer drifts with the weather.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: A great-circle course is the shortest path on a sphere between two latitudes and longitudes. The initial bearing is the direction you start, and it can change as you travel. Reverse bearing is the direction back. These tools use that spherical estimate. They do not follow roads and they do not download tiles.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: A track log is a list of your own points, saved on this device only after you consent. Distance is the sum of the great-circle legs. Elapsed time is counted only when those points carry timestamps. It is not someone else's path, and it is not sent anywhere unless you say so in your own words.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: Landscape navigation here is terrain, water, coast, and sky: distance, bearing, waypoints, and a track you record yourself. It deliberately has no city map, no street list, and no points of interest that go stale as towns change. If you need a town, use a map you brought, not this store.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: Yehsa medical entries are offline reference labels for a personal survival agent. They are not a diagnosis, a prescription, or a substitute for emergency services. In an emergency, contact local emergency services.
passages.title: reference

passages.context: Serious bleeding needs direct pressure with clean cloth and urgent human help. This note does not teach surgery or medication dosing.
passages.title: reference

passages.context: Clean water matters before wound rinsing or rehydration. Boil water when you can. This is a field reminder, not clinical instruction.
passages.title: reference

passages.context: A mosquito bite is usually a small itchy spot. Wash it with clean water. Swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing, needs a person and emergency services, not a plant.
passages.title: reference

passages.context: A tourniquet is a last resort for life-threatening limb bleeding, when direct pressure with clean cloth does not stop the blood. Put it between the wound and the heart, and note the time it went on. Do not loosen it in the field. This is not surgery and not a substitute for emergency care.
passages.title: reference

passages.context: Frostbite is frozen skin, often fingers, toes, ears, or the nose. Get to shelter and put on dry layers. Do not rub the skin, and do not rub snow on it. Warm it against healthy skin or in warm, not hot, water, and do not walk on a thawed foot if you still must travel; this is not a substitute for emergency care.
passages.title: reference

passages.context: A splint keeps a suspected broken bone still, such as a broken arm or leg. Pad it, include the joints above and below, and tie it snug enough to stop motion without cutting off circulation. Skin beyond it should stay warm and able to feel. Do not set the bone; this is not surgery or a substitute for emergency care.
passages.title: reference

passages.context: Cover skin and avoid standing water when you can, so fewer mosquitoes bite. A plant on the skin does not replace that, and it does not treat diseases mosquitoes can carry.
passages.title: camp

passages.context: Camp site: pick flat ground out of a drainage, off the ridge, and clear of dead limbs. Face the opening away from the night wind. A spot near a stream is handy and also a flood risk, so step uphill a little. This is planning, not a permit to camp where rules forbid it.
passages.title: camp

passages.context: Sleep: insulation under you matters as much as the cover over you. Change out of wet clothes before you lie down, and keep a dry layer in the bag. Food and scented items stay outside the sleep spot. A closed shelter still needs air. This note does not treat cold injury.
passages.title: camp

passages.context: Kitchen: cook and store food downwind of where you sleep, and seal it so animals are not fed. Drown the fire or stove and feel for heat before you leave. Strain cloudy water, then boil it, before it goes in the pot. Known food only. This is not a foraging menu.
passages.title: camp

passages.context: Sanitation: carry waste out when the land requires it. Otherwise dig a small cathole well away from water, camp, and trails, then cover it. Soap stays out of the creek. Hands are cleaned away from the stream. This is a hygiene reminder, not a medical treatment.
passages.title: camp

passages.context: Leave the site: pack out what you carried in, put back natural cover you moved, and drown the fire until it is cold. The next person should not be able to tell you cooked there. A waypoint you saved stays on your device. Erasing the camp from the land is the point.
passages.title: camp

passages.context: Food: eat known cultivated food or packaged rations before foraging. Do not taste unknown plants, mushrooms, or unfamiliar meat. Herbology notes in this repo are cautions, not a menu. Hunger is not a reason to experiment.
passages.title: food

passages.context: Pack food you already eat, with the first night's portion on top of the bag. Eat small amounts through the day. A pot and a spoon you have used at home beat a new wild food. This sets no calorie target and no meal plan for a clinic.
passages.title: food

passages.context: Cook known food until it is hot through, and keep raw scraps away from the cooked pot. Seal or hang leftovers so animals are not invited to where you sleep. A bulging can or a sour smell means you discard it. Do not taste food to decide if it has turned.
passages.title: food

passages.context: Berries, fish, and greens are a local-rules question, and only for kinds you already know from a source outside this note. If you are not sure, it does not go in your mouth. Mushrooms are not a trial. Cultivated food is the plan. Wild food is not a backup menu and not a dose guide.
passages.title: food

passages.context: Navigation: the sun rises generally east and sets generally west. A map and compass beat guesswork. If you are lost, staying put and making yourself visible is often safer than wandering. This is not a complete orienteering manual.
passages.title: navigation

passages.context: Walk to a landmark you can name, a boulder, a saddle, or a distinct tree, then pick the next. Count paces on a stretch you already measured so distance is a number. Stop while the last sure point is still clear. Turning around is a plan, not a failure.
passages.title: navigation

passages.context: A shoreline, a ridge, or a stream can be a handrail you keep beside you. Know which side you are on, and which bend means you have gone too far. A handrail is a landscape line. It is not a street. If it splits and you cannot say which branch, you stop.
passages.title: navigation

passages.context: If you are unsure, sit and sketch a circle of possible places instead of a hopeful dot. Signal from an open spot. Move only toward a feature you can name, in daylight, and camp if dusk is close. These notes do not replace a map you can read, and they do not invent a trail.
passages.title: navigation

passages.context: Shelter and fire: get out of wind and wet ground first. A small contained fire needs clear fuel, a safe distance from brush, and a way to put it out. Do not light a fire where local rules forbid it. This is a planning note, not a wilderness course.
passages.title: shelter_fire

passages.context: Pick the site before the flame. Choose ground that sheds rain, above a flood line, and clear of dead trees that can drop limbs. Face the opening away from the wind. A finger-width of dry insulation under you holds more heat than a tall roof. This is planning, not a building code.
passages.title: shelter_fire

passages.context: Build a fire only where rules allow it, on scraped mineral soil, with fuel upwind and a way to drown it. Start with tinder and pencil twigs, and add thicker wood after the flame is honest. Feel the ashes cold before you leave. A banned day or a hard wind means no flame.
passages.title: shelter_fire

passages.context: Without a fire, stay dry, covered, and off the ground, and keep the wind off your back. Any flame inside a closed shelter can foul the air, so leave a vent and do not sleep against a heater. Wet clothes next to the skin steal heat even in mild air. This does not treat a cold injury.
passages.title: shelter_fire

passages.context: Signaling: three of anything (whistle blasts, bright flashes, fires) is a common distress pattern. A mirror or light aimed at rescuers is a signal, not a weapon. Tell another person where you are going before you travel.
passages.title: signaling

passages.context: A whistle carries farther than a shout and spends less breath. Three short blasts, a pause, then three again is the pattern to repeat. If you hear a reply, answer the same way and stay where you can be seen. Yelling until you are hoarse does not mark your location.
passages.title: signaling

passages.context: Put bright gear in an open sight line, in a straight line or a large X. Flash a mirror toward a ridge or an aircraft in short groups of three, then stop so you do not dazzle someone close. Day smoke and a night flame are signals only where fire is legal and contained.
passages.title: signaling

passages.context: An arrow of stones or packs can show the way you left, if you must leave, and only where the sky can see it. Tell a person your route, your return time, and the color of your pack before you go. If you are unsure, signal and stay visible. This is how to be found, not a radio trick.
passages.title: signaling

passages.context: Tools and cordage: a knife, cord, and container solve more camp problems than improvising from scratch. Keep edges covered. Natural cord from bark or roots only comes from plants you are allowed to cut and can identify. This is not a weapons guide.
passages.title: tools_cordage

passages.context: Use the knife away from your body, on a firm surface, and sheath it when you move. A dull edge slips, so a small stone belongs with the blade. Do not throw it, and do not pry with the only knife you have. A covered edge does not cut the bottle in the pack. This is handling, not a fight.
passages.title: tools_cordage

passages.context: Carry cord you already trust before you strip a living plant. A few meters can hang a pot clear of flame, tie a shelter ridge, or repair a strap. Learn two knots you can also undo. Wet natural fiber swells and can jam a knot you tied while it was dry.
passages.title: tools_cordage

passages.context: A needle, a little tape, and cord stop a small tear from becoming a lost strap or a split handle. Brighten a tool handle so it shows against leaves. A lighter in a dry bag is the simple spark; practice it at home. This note does not teach you to burn the country.
passages.title: tools_cordage

passages.context: Water: carry known-safe water when you can. If you must treat water in the field, boiling is the straightforward heat method. Cloudy water should be settled or strained before boiling. This is an offline reminder, not a guarantee the water is safe, and not a substitute for emergency services.
passages.title: water

passages.context: Containers matter. A closed bottle or a pot you can heat beats a leaky bag. Keep the drinking bottle capped and off the ground, and refill it when you pass a source you mean to treat. A spare empty container is how you carry water away from the source.
passages.title: water

passages.context: Where to look: green growth on a dry slope, a dark seep, or a stream in the lowest line of a valley are clues. Flowing water is a better clue than a still pool. Clues are not proof. Settle the grit, then boil, and still treat the result as uncertain.
passages.title: water

passages.context: Snow and ice need melting before you drink them, and melting spends fuel you may need for warmth. Eating snow when you are already cold cools you further. Salt water and urine are not drinking water. This reminder sets no liter quota and no chemical dose.
passages.title: water

passages.context: Carry more than the first hour seems to need, then drink small amounts through the day instead of emptying the bottle at once. In heat, rest in shade before you feel dizzy. If someone stops sweating or grows confused, stop travel and get human help. This is not a medical threshold.
passages.title: water

passages.context: Weather: dark building clouds, sudden wind, and thunder mean you should leave high ground and open water. Cold plus wet clothing steals heat. This note does not forecast a local storm.
passages.title: weather

passages.context: Read the sky you have. A hard wind shift, a fast drop in temperature, and a dark towering cloud are reasons to leave ridges and lone tall trees. A shorter gap between flash and thunder only means the cell is closer. Do not wait for a forecast you cannot make. Get lower.
passages.title: weather

passages.context: Wind that rises and holds one direction often comes before rain. Face the shelter away from it, and weight anything that can blow away. Blowing dust is a reason to seek a low sturdy spot, not a hilltop. This note is not a warning siren and not a local forecast.
passages.title: weather

passages.context: A clear night is often colder than a cloudy one. Put the rain layer on before you are soaked, and keep a hat where you can reach it. Stop early enough to camp in daylight. The plan is to be dry before the wind arrives, not after.
passages.title: weather

passages.context: Heat is a travel cost: still air, a high sun, and no shade. Move earlier and later, rest at midday, and cover your head. Pushing on through dizziness is a reason to stop and get help, not a goal. This note does not set a temperature rule.
passages.title: weather
